candidate.title: Coast and inland: compare places using evidence

prompts: Without the worked example, explain: Use geographical vocabulary and a labelled sketch to compare coastal and inland landscapes in Liberia.
Without the worked example, explain: Support a comparison with relevant text evidence while distinguishing observations from unsupported generalizations.

pedagogy.rationale: Read a short factual geography summary, compare explicitly fictional local observations and justify a community decision. Distinguish physical description from a guarantee about people or safety.

prerequisiteAssumptions: Read a short passage or direct a reader/scribe.
Recognize sea, land, hill and river in words or a sketch.

misconceptions.description: Every inland location is assumed to be high or mountainous.
misconceptions.response: Inland means away from the coast. A broad terrain description does not determine every local elevation.

misconceptions.description: One observation or place description is treated as evidence about all communities.
misconceptions.response: Name the place and observation, limit the conclusion to that evidence and seek additional observations.

misconceptions.description: Coastal or inland is treated as enough evidence to select a safe site.
misconceptions.response: Compare the actual site, path and local observations. A region label alone does not establish safety.

misconceptions.description: General coast-to-inland landform descriptions are treated as exact county boundaries.
misconceptions.response: Use an administrative map for county boundaries. A physical sketch does not establish those lines.

misconceptions.description: Evidence about a dry room or a clear path is treated as proving the other requirement too.
misconceptions.response: Check each requirement separately. Room and route observations answer different questions.

scenes.title: Read, picture and question the landscape
scenes.learnerAction: Read or listen, make a labelled sketch and ask one question about a place you know.

content.body: Read the geography passage. Say what coast and inland mean before comparing them. Sketch sea, coast and inland land. Label your sketch as a simple model without a scale. A sketch helps explain a relationship; it does not locate an actual school.

accessibility.textAlternative: Read the geography passage. Say what coast and inland mean before comparing them. Sketch sea, coast and inland land. Label your sketch as a simple model without a scale. A sketch helps explain a relationship; it does not locate an actual school. Reading Liberia's landscape. Liberia lies in West Africa beside the Atlantic Ocean. Coastal means near the sea. Inland means farther from the coast. Liberia has coastal lowlands, with hills and higher land farther inland. These broad descriptions do not give every place the same shape. A plain is a broad area of fairly level land. A plateau is higher land with a fairly level surface. A physical region describes landscape features. It is not the same as a county boundary. Read a map's key before using its symbols.

blocks.title: Reading Liberia's landscape
paragraphs: Liberia lies in West Africa beside the Atlantic Ocean. Coastal means near the sea. Inland means farther from the coast. Liberia has coastal lowlands, with hills and higher land farther inland. These broad descriptions do not give every place the same shape.

A plain is a broad area of fairly level land. A plateau is higher land with a fairly level surface. A physical region describes landscape features. It is not the same as a county boundary. Read a map's key before using its symbols.

scenes.title: Model a careful comparison
scenes.learnerAction: Underline the difference in the model. Circle the words that limit its claim.

content.body: A careful comparison names a difference and explains its evidence. Coastal describes closeness to the sea. Inland describes being farther from the coast. Neither word gives an exact height. A county is an administrative area; a physical description concerns landscape. Do not draw county borders from these words.

accessibility.textAlternative: A careful comparison names a difference and explains its evidence. Coastal describes closeness to the sea. Inland describes being farther from the coast. Neither word gives an exact height. A county is an administrative area; a physical description concerns landscape. Do not draw county borders from these words. How can we compare without claiming too much? Step 1: Name the feature: distance from the coast. Step 2: Compare: a coastal location is nearer the sea than an inland location. Step 3: Limit: this description alone does not give an exact height or every person's work.

scenes.title: Find evidence and reject an overstatement
scenes.learnerAction: Check the geographical claim, then explain what further information a real map would need.

content.body: Use the passage to check a claim about inland land. A description can name several landforms without describing every location. Read all options before choosing. Explain which words make a claim broader than its evidence.

prompts.prompt: What map information would you need to compare two actual locations rather than a simple sketch?

hints: Look for the different landforms named in the passage.
The word every needs evidence about every location, not a broad description.

accessibility.textAlternative: Use the passage to check a claim about inland land. A description can name several landforms without describing every location. Read all options before choosing. Explain which words make a claim broader than its evidence. Which claim fits the passage? Options: A coast-to-inland sketch gives every county border exactly.; Inland places can have different landforms; a local map gives more detail.; Every inland home stands on a mountain.. What map information would you need to compare two actual locations rather than a simple sketch?

options.text: A coast-to-inland sketch gives every county border exactly.
options.feedback: Physical descriptions do not supply administrative boundaries or a geographical scale.

options.text: Inland places can have different landforms; a local map gives more detail.
options.feedback: This respects the broad description without treating every inland place as identical.

options.text: Every inland home stands on a mountain.
options.feedback: Inland describes position away from the coast, not one height for every home.

scenes.title: Read two community records
scenes.learnerAction: Select two relevant details, explain their different meanings and name one missing observation.

content.body: Read both invented records. Separate a room observation from a path observation. A dry room and an accessible path answer different questions. Select the evidence needed to discuss Club A. Keep unobserved conditions visible rather than guessing about them.

hints: Find one sentence about the room and one about the path.
A club's location label does not replace the actual observations.

accessibility.textAlternative: Read both invented records. Separate a room observation from a path observation. A dry room and an accessible path answer different questions. Select the evidence needed to discuss Club A. Keep unobserved conditions visible rather than guessing about them. Two invented reading-club records. These reading clubs and observations are invented for this lesson. Club A is near the coast. Its covered room stayed dry during two observed showers. Water covered part of its path during one shower. Nobody checked the path after dark. Club B is inland beside a river. Its room had a leaking roof. Its path stayed clear during both observed showers. Nobody checked the river after prolonged rain. Both clubs want books kept dry and a route that an adult can check. Club A's invented record. The covered room stayed dry during two observed showers. Water covered part of the path during one shower. Club A is near the coast. Which two details support discussing the room and route separately? Which reason best supports checking Club A's path? Options: Every coastal path must always be unusable.; Its room was dry, so the path needs no attention.; Part of its path was covered by water in an observed shower..

blocks.title: Two invented reading-club records
paragraphs: These reading clubs and observations are invented for this lesson. Club A is near the coast. Its covered room stayed dry during two observed showers. Water covered part of its path during one shower. Nobody checked the path after dark.

Club B is inland beside a river. Its room had a leaking roof. Its path stayed clear during both observed showers. Nobody checked the river after prolonged rain. Both clubs want books kept dry and a route that an adult can check.

blocks.question: Which two details support discussing the room and route separately?

sentences.text: The covered room stayed dry during two observed showers.
sentences.why: This concerns the room during the observed conditions, not every possible storm.

sentences.text: Water covered part of the path during one shower.
sentences.why: This concerns access and needs attention even when the room stayed dry.

sentences.text: Club A is near the coast.
sentences.why: The location label alone does not show whether the room or route meets the club's needs.

items.prompt: Which reason best supports checking Club A's path?

options.text: Every coastal path must always be unusable.
options.feedback: The record concerns one path and one observed condition, not every coastal route.

options.text: Its room was dry, so the path needs no attention.
options.feedback: A dry room does not establish that the route to it is clear.

options.text: Part of its path was covered by water in an observed shower.
options.feedback: A specific route observation is relevant to access.

scenes.title: Compare with two kinds of evidence
scenes.learnerAction: Write a short comparison with evidence from both clubs and a limit of the records.

content.body: Work independently with both records. Compare the rooms and compare the paths. Keep their coastal or inland positions in your explanation. Use each observation only for the question it answers. Explain one thing that neither record establishes.

prompts.prompt: Write 30 to 60 words comparing the two rooms and paths. Include both places, two relevant observations and something still unknown.

scenes.title: Test the strength of a claim
scenes.learnerAction: Evaluate both claims independently. Explain how to make a conclusion match its evidence.

content.body: A classmate says Club A's dry room proves that every coastal building stays dry. Decide whether the conclusion follows. Then consider Club B's clear path. Does that observation settle every question about an inland site? Explain the difference between a recorded observation and a much wider claim.

prompts.prompt: Explain why Club B's clear path does not settle the roof or prolonged-rain questions.

accessibility.textAlternative: A classmate says Club A's dry room proves that every coastal building stays dry. Decide whether the conclusion follows. Then consider Club B's clear path. Does that observation settle every question about an inland site? Explain the difference between a recorded observation and a much wider claim. Which conclusion is supported about Club A's room? Options: No inland building can stay dry.; It stayed dry during the two showers described.; All coastal buildings stay dry in every storm.. Explain why Club B's clear path does not settle the roof or prolonged-rain questions.

scenes.title: Weigh a counterargument
scenes.learnerAction: Identify the faulty reason and propose a condition for a defensible recommendation.

content.body: A fictional pupil chooses Club B only because it is inland. Another notices its leaking roof. A reasoned recommendation answers that counterargument. Use observations to propose what must be repaired or checked. Do not turn a provisional choice into a guarantee.

prompts.prompt: Give a provisional recommendation or explain why neither site is ready. Answer one counterargument with evidence.

accessibility.textAlternative: A fictional pupil chooses Club B only because it is inland. Another notices its leaking roof. A reasoned recommendation answers that counterargument. Use observations to propose what must be repaired or checked. Do not turn a provisional choice into a guarantee. A club needs dry book storage and a route an adult can check. A fictional pupil wrote: Club B is inland. Therefore its room and path must meet every need. Which response best repairs the reasoning? Options: Use the roof and route observations, then name a repair or further check.; Choose Club A just because it is coastal instead.; Ignore the roof because the path was clear.. Give a provisional recommendation or explain why neither site is ready. Answer one counterargument with evidence.

steps: Therefore its room and path must meet every need.

correction: Compare each site against both needs, answer a counterargument and state what remains to check.

scenes.title: Use the method beyond these records
scenes.learnerAction: Create an evidence checklist, explain whom you would ask and revise one earlier claim.

content.body: Plan questions for a reading club in your community or another African community. Use the same needs, but seek local evidence. A similar landscape does not prove identical conditions. Include people who use different routes or need step-free access. No trip or inspection is required today.

prompts.prompt: Write three questions about a proposed room and route. Identify evidence each question needs. Explain why a plan from another country should be checked locally. Revise one sentence of your comparison using what you learned.
